questions.question: Define a magnetic field, and compare it with the gravitational and electric fields by stating what each field acts on and whether each can repel.
questions.expected_answer: A magnetic field is a region in space where another magnet or a ferromagnetic material experiences a force. Gravitational field: a region where a mass experiences a force — attraction only. Electric field: a region where a charge experiences a force — attracts or repels, and single charges can exist alone. Magnetic field: acts on magnets and ferromagnetic materials (iron, steel, cobalt, nickel) — attracts or repels, but its poles never exist separately.

questions.question: A bar magnet is sawn in half. Describe the result and explain it using the domain model.
questions.expected_answer: Each half is a complete magnet with both a north and a south pole — a new pole appears at each cut face. Explanation: magnetism comes from domains — small regions where the tiny magnetic fields of electrons are aligned. In a magnetised bar the domains are aligned throughout the whole material, so any piece cut from it still contains aligned domains and is a complete two-poled magnet. There is no 'north substance' at one end to isolate; an isolated pole (monopole) has never been observed.

questions.question: State the four rules for drawing magnetic field lines, and describe the field patterns for two facing opposite poles and two facing like poles.
questions.expected_answer: Rules: (1) outside the magnet, lines run from north to south with arrows; (2) closer spacing means a stronger field — densest at the poles; (3) lines never cross; (4) the field is three-dimensional even though drawings are flat. Opposite poles facing: lines run in a dense bridge from one magnet's north across the gap into the other's south — the pattern of attraction. Like poles facing: lines bend sharply away from the gap and refuse to connect, leaving a neutral point between the poles where the fields cancel — the pattern of repulsion.
